title: The Patient Dictation Agent
promise: Watch it build; then it's yours.
agent: A dictation agent built from the zero agent: the most basic voice agent — a transcriber — plus a segmenter that files a word-timed stream into markdown chunks on a pulse, under a mode toggle. This playthrough builds its Patient mode: the one that keeps listening while you stop, think, and look out the window.

source.engine: segmenter.js — a faithful port of segmenter.py, verified against the prototype test-for-test and chunk-for-chunk on identical streams (VERIFY.md)
source.recordDerivedFrom: the 2026-10-12 design record and the prototype's own measured runs (ground_truth.py over fixtures.py's seeded streams)

config.note: Modes are configurations of one block — a toggle, not three products. The live pad's stream is simulated text with word timings, not audio: the segmenter consumes word-timed streams, and a microphone front end is a separate block that was deliberately not built.

honesty: The chat is sourced, not scripted: Casey's turns render his recorded 2026-10-12 voice-block design — the building-block sketch as decomposed at the time under his ramble protocol, kept short and fragmentary in its shape; the 'go long' dispatch and the seeds doctrine framed the build but are not staged as turns. The brief and builder turns condense the actual spec (segmenter.py, the block README) and the verified receipts (the 16 tests, demo.py, modes/RESULTS.md). Every measured number in the state rail is sliced from the prototype's recorded runs by make_playthrough.py and asserted against them; none is invented. The tree lists the block's source files (lockfile and installed dependencies not shown). The end state is the working segmenter: the pad runs segmenter.js, the port verified in VERIFY.md.

steps.title: The blank page
steps.narration: The zero agent starts as a blank page — no files, no memory, nothing spent. Everything after this is additions. This time the addition is an ear.

steps.title: The most basic voice agent
steps.narration: The block is a transcriber and nothing more — plus the tools a transcriber needs to be useful: a segmenter that files speech into chunks, and an assembler that marks them up honestly.

chat.speaker: Casey
chat.text: the most basic voice agent. just a transcriber — transcribe english speech to text.
chat.note: The sketch — 2026-10-12, rendered from the record made at the time.

chat.speaker: Casey
chat.text: but split it into markdown chunks — no more than about three-quarters of a page. and an assembler that puts the codings on the words, from how the transcriber worked.

chat.speaker: The brief
chat.text: The block consumes a word-timed stream — every word carrying start and end times, as an STT engine produces it. The segmenter accumulates words and emits markdown chunks; the assembler adds only the markup the timing signal supports: paragraph breaks at long pauses, sentence casing, emphasis on words held notably long.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: ✅ segmenter.py — a Segmenter with feed and flush, emitting markdown chunks. The word-timed stream is the contract; the microphone is a different block, deliberately not built.

fourth.label: words per chunk, at most (~¾ page)

steps.title: The pulse — three triggers and a best break
steps.narration: The block runs on a pulse: three triggers, any of them fires. And when size or time fires, the cut doesn't land where the trigger did — it lands at the best break the buffer offers.

chat.speaker: Casey
chat.text: put it on a pulse. emit every minute or so, every three-quarter page, or when there's a gap of more than about five seconds. the gaps are where someone can say something in between — to make it stop.
chat.note: The sketch — 2026-10-12, rendered from the record made at the time.

chat.speaker: Casey
chat.text: and don't cut where the trigger lands — pick the best-break. the cue is the pause: somebody took a breath, a sentence ended.

chat.speaker: The brief
chat.text: Three triggers, any fires. GAP — a pause before the next word longer than 5 s ends the chunk on the spot, and the gap is recorded. SIZE — 500 words. TIME — 60 s inside the chunk. SIZE and TIME pick the best break instead: score every boundary, min(pause, 3 s) + 2 if the word ends a sentence; ties go to the later boundary; the remainder starts the next chunk. Plus tick(now) — a wall-clock call, so a live deployment can learn that a silence has happened without waiting for speech to resume.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: ✅ demo, the segmenter against a naive fixed-window cutter: 0% of chunks end mid-sentence, on every speech fixture — the naive cutter ends 82–100% of its chunks mid-sentence. Mean pause at the chosen break: 0.87 s, against the naive 0.21 s.

steps.title: Sixteen tests
steps.narration: Before the block is trusted with anyone's voice, its invariants become tests: nothing lost, nothing oversize, nothing out of order — and the planted break at word 480 must beat the trigger point at 500.

chat.speaker: The brief
chat.text: The invariants, as tests. No word is ever lost, on any stream shape. No chunk passes 500 words. Chunks stay time-ordered. The best-break test plants a pause and a sentence end at word 480 of 500 — the cut must land at 480. The tick test: silent at 2.35 s of gap, emitted at 5.35 s, never twice.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: ✅ 16/16 tests pass. Stop-and-think: 11 gap chunks for 12 bursts, every end_pause over 5 s. Metronome: the time trigger only — its 2.7 s pauses stay under the gap gate, as designed. Zero word loss across all five fixtures.

steps.title: Modes are a toggle, not three products
steps.narration: Same block, three cadence-and-initiative configurations. The ask was never three agents — it was one agent with a toggle, because neither eager nor patient is better. They are different situations.

chat.speaker: Casey
chat.text: the modes are a toggle, not three products. eager — the other chatbot: stop talking and it answers right away; you have to keep feeding it words. patient — you will keep on listening: i can walk twenty minutes saying not much — stop, think, look out the window. async-parallel — it works while i keep talking, its work on screen as it happens, and i can interrupt or nudge it mid-stream.
chat.note: The sketch — 2026-10-12, rendered from the record made at the time.

chat.speaker: The brief
chat.text: One block, three configs. EAGER: gap 0.8 s, page 120 words, clock 15 s. PATIENT: gap effectively never, page 500, clock 20 minutes. ASYNC-PARALLEL: the base cadence — gap 5 s, page 500, clock 60 s — plus a work model: each emitted chunk starts a job, progress surfaces live, and a gap with a job in flight is a nudge point. The simulator replays identical streams through all three, emissions timed by wall-clock ticks as a live system would notice them.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: ✅ modes/simulate.py — the three configs over the same word-timed streams, with a nominal 0.3 s processing delay on responses. Model latency is out of scope: this measures the block's cadence, not a model.

steps.title: The 20-minute walk, measured
steps.narration: The fixture is Casey's walk: 886 words over 19 minutes, talk in bursts, silence while he looks out the window. Patient holds everything — 499 words at the peak — answers twice, and loses nothing.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: ✅ the sparse walk, three ways. Eager: 45 responses, the first at 10 s. Patient: exactly 2 responses in 19 minutes, the first at 549 s; up to 499 words sat buffered and unacknowledged — and nothing was lost; every word was eventually filed. Async: 10 chunks, first response at 64 s, all 9 jobs finished before he stopped talking.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: The reading of it: patient is total recall and zero companionship. For nine minutes there is no signal that anyone is listening. It is a recorder with good filing — which is exactly what the walking mode was asked to be.

steps.title: Eager's rudeness is positional
steps.narration: Eager has the same 0.8 s threshold everywhere. In flowing speech it talks over the speaker constantly; between thoughts it almost never does. The rudeness was never in the number — it's in where the pauses are.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: ✅ talked-over counts, by stream shape. Flowing monologue: eager starts talking into the next sentence 64 of 75 times — every sentence-final breath of 0.85 s or more reads as a full stop. Stop-and-think dictation: 4 of 50 — there it answers inside the pauses and the conversation feels snappy.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: The lesson the seed bought: eagerness is a property of where the pauses are, not of the threshold. A mode tuned on dictation will be rude in conversation — measurable before it ships, not after.

steps.title: The wall clock earns its keep
steps.narration: A segmenter that only learns about a silence when speech resumes answers one thought late, every time. The tick — one line of API from step 2 — turns out to be load-bearing.

chat.speaker: The brief
chat.text: Stream-driven endpointing has a systematic lag: the gap is discovered at the next word, so the response to a finished thought waits for the start of the next one. The wall-clock tick notices the silence while it is happening. Any real deployment of this block needs the tick, or an equivalent watchdog.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: ✅ measured on the walk: async, stream-only, answered first at 169 s. With tick() checking the clock: 64 s. And the work didn't just come earlier — it moved into the silences themselves, which is where a walking speaker can actually use it.

steps.title: The clock beats the page
steps.narration: The ¾-page rule was the headline of the sketch. The arithmetic disagrees — politely, and with receipts: at speaking speed, the minute always arrives before the page does.

chat.speaker: The builder
chat.text: ✅ the count: 500 words takes about two and a half minutes to say out loud. So under the full cadence, continuous speech trips the 60-second TIME trigger at roughly 180 words — about a quarter page — long before SIZE can fire. The ¾-page rule binds only when word events arrive faster than real time: batch and file transcription.

chat.speaker: Casey
chat.text: so is the three-quarter page a batch rule? or does the live cap shrink to meet the clock?
chat.note: His open question — recorded, not resolved.

steps.title: Working state — it's yours, and it's listening
steps.narration: The same segmenter, a second runtime, and then the handoff: the pad below runs the JavaScript port of this exact block, verified test-for-test against the Python above. Patient is the default. It will hold its tongue through your pauses — flip it to Eager and feel the difference.

chat.speaker: The brief
chat.text: Same rules, second runtime: the segmenter in TypeScript on Cloudflare Workers — triggers and scoring identical, markup left to the renderer. State in an in-memory map; the Durable Object production path sketched, not bound. Nothing deploys without a word.
